subject: math
title: Exponents and Order of Operations
instructions: Work every problem on paper first and show each step. Then type your answer and press Check. You get two tries on each question. Type a power with the ^ key: 3^4 means 3⁴. For an answer below zero, type the minus sign first.

sections.name: Part A: Review
sections.desc: Two problems from older lessons. Picture a number line for the integers. Line up the digits for the multiplication.

items.q: Add or subtract. Picture a number line: adding moves right and subtracting moves left.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The temperature was −3°C at dawn. It rose 8 degrees by noon, then fell 11 degrees by midnight. What was the temperature at midnight, in degrees Celsius?

items.q: Multiply. Write the partial products on paper before you add them.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A school orders 24 boxes of pencils. Each box holds 144 pencils. How many pencils is that in all?

sections.name: Part B: Reading and writing powers
sections.desc: The exponent tells how many times the base is used as a factor.

items.q: Look at the power 5³.
a: a) The base is the number that gets multiplied. Here the base is 5.
b) The exponent counts the factors. 5³ = 5 × 5 × 5, so the exponent is 3.
items.hint: One number is the factor that repeats. The other number counts how many times it repeats.

items.q: Write each product as a power. Type a power with the ^ key, like 3^4.
a: a) 7 is a factor 5 times, so the power is 7⁵.
b) 2 is a factor 7 times, so the power is 2⁷.
items.hint: Count the factors. That count is the exponent, and the repeated number is the base.

items.q: Which expression shows what 4⁵ means?
a: 4 × 5 = 20, which multiplies the base by the exponent. That is a different number.
5 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 625, which is 5⁴ with the base and the exponent swapped.
items.hint: The exponent counts factors. It does not multiply the base.

items.q: Write each phrase as a power. Type a power with the ^ key, like 3^4.
a: a) Cubed means exponent 3, so the power is 9³.
b) Fourth power means exponent 4, so the power is 6⁴.
c) Fifth power means exponent 5, so the power is 10⁵.
items.hint: The number named first is the base. The words after it tell how many times the base is used as a factor.

items.q: Answer each question about powers.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A power with exponent 3 means 11 × 11 × 11. What is its base?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A power has base 4, and its value is also 4. What is its exponent?

a: a) The repeated factor is the base, so the base is 11.
items.hint: The repeated factor is the base. For part b, write out a few powers of 4 and find their values.

sections.name: Part C: Finding the value of a power
sections.desc: Write out the factors and multiply one step at a time. A power is repeated multiplication. Do not multiply the base by the exponent.

items.q: Find the value of each square.
items.hint: A square is the number times itself.

items.q: Find the value of each cube.
items.hint: A cube uses the base as a factor three times. Multiply two of them, then multiply by the base once more.

items.q: These three look alike but have different values. Find each one.
items.hint: Only one of these is a plain multiplication. For each power, write out the factors first.

items.q: Find the value of each power.
items.hint: Multiply one factor at a time and write each product down before you go on.

items.q: Look at the pattern in the table. Each time the exponent goes down by 1, the value is divided by the base, which is 2.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Follow the pattern one more step. What is the value of 2⁰?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The same pattern works for other bases. 10² is 100 and 10¹ is 10. What is the value of 10⁰?

a: a) 4 ÷ 2 = 2, so the value of 2¹ is 2.
b) 2 ÷ 2 = 1, so the value of 2⁰ is 1.
c) 10 ÷ 10 = 1, so the value of 10⁰ is 1.
Answers: a) 2, b) 1, c) 1. A base other than 0 with exponent 0 always has the value 1.
items.hint: Each step to the right, divide by the base. For part c the base is 10, not 2.

items.q: Find each missing number.
a: a) 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32, which uses five 2s, so the exponent is 5.
items.hint: Test small numbers one at a time. For part a, keep doubling and count the 2s you use.

sections.name: Part D: Powers of 10
sections.desc: The exponent on 10 tells how many zeros follow the 1.

items.q: Find the value of each power of 10.
items.hint: Count the zeros as you write them, in groups of three.

items.q: Write each number as a power of 10. Type a power with the ^ key, like 10^2.
a: a) 10,000,000 has 7 zeros, so the power is 10⁷.
b) 1,000,000,000 has 9 zeros, so the power is 10⁹.
items.hint: Count the zeros after the 1. Count in groups of three so that none are skipped.

items.q: Find each value. Find the power of 10 first, then multiply.
items.hint: The exponent comes before the multiplying. Only the 10 is raised to the power.

items.q: Each number is written in expanded form with powers of 10. Find its value.
items.hint: Find each power of 10, multiply, then add the pieces. Watch for a place value that has no piece.

sections.name: Part E: Comparing powers
sections.desc: Find each value before you compare. A bigger exponent does not always make a bigger number.

items.q: Find both values, then choose the greater power.
a: c) 243 is greater than 125, so 3⁵ is greater.
items.hint: Write out all the factors for each power. Count them before you multiply.

items.q: Find both values, then compare.
a: c) Both values are 256, so the two powers are equal.
Answers: a) 256, b) 256, c) They are equal
items.hint: Keep a running product on paper. For the second power, keep doubling and count each 2.

items.q: Find the value of each power: 2⁵, 3³, 5² and 6¹. Then type the four values in order from least to greatest, with commas between them.
a: From least to greatest the values are 6, 25, 27, 32.
items.hint: Find all four values first and write them down. Then sort the values, not the exponents.

sections.name: Part F: Order of operations
sections.desc: Parentheses first. Then multiply and divide from left to right. Then add and subtract from left to right.

items.q: Find the value of each expression.
items.hint: Circle each multiplication and division. Do those before any adding or subtracting.

items.q: Work from left to right. Find the value of each expression.
items.hint: Multiplying and dividing have the same rank, so take them in the order they appear. The same goes for adding and subtracting.

items.q: Find the value of each expression. Do the work inside the parentheses first.
items.hint: Inside parentheses the same order still applies: multiply before you add.

items.q: Find the value of each expression. Rewrite the whole expression after each step.
items.hint: Number your steps: parentheses, then multiply and divide from the left, then add and subtract from the left.

items.q: Sam and Lena each found the value of 8 + 12 ÷ 4 − 2. Sam got 3. Lena got 9.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: What is the correct value of 8 + 12 ÷ 4 − 2?

a: b) Sam added first and got 20. Then 20 ÷ 4 is 5, and 5 − 2 is 3. The division had to come before the addition.
Answers: a) 9, b) He added 8 + 12 before he divided
items.hint: Find the division. It comes before the addition and the subtraction.

sections.name: Part G: Order of operations with exponents
sections.desc: Find the value of each power right after the parentheses, before you multiply, divide, add or subtract.

items.q: Find the value of each expression.
items.hint: An exponent belongs only to the number it sits on, unless parentheses group more.

items.q: Find the value of each expression.
items.hint: List the powers first and replace each one with its value. Then multiply and divide before you add or subtract.

items.q: Some of these values are below zero. Find each value.
items.hint: Find the powers first. When you subtract a larger number from a smaller one, the result is below zero. Picture the number line.

items.q: Find the value of each expression.
items.hint: Replace every power with its value before you do anything else.

items.q: Find the value of each expression. Take one step per line.
items.hint: Start inside the parentheses. Inside them, a power still comes before the other operations.

items.q: Turn the words into an expression on paper, then find its value.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Add 4 and 5, then square the result.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Square 5, then subtract the product of 3 and 6.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Subtract 2 squared from 2 cubed, then multiply the result by 10 squared.

items.hint: Put parentheses around the part that the words say to do first.

sections.name: Part H: Real jobs
sections.desc: Each problem ends in a decision. Find the numbers first, then decide, then give the reason with the numbers in it.

items.q: A neighbor offers two ways to pay you for 5 days of yard work. Plan A pays $40 every day. Plan B pays $2 on day 1, and the pay doubles every day after that: day 2 pays $4, day 3 pays $8, and so on.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Total pay for the 5 days under Plan A

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Total pay for the 5 days under Plan B

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which plan should you take for this 5 day job?

ans.model: Plan A pays $200 in total. Plan B pays only $62 in total over 5 days, so Plan A pays $138 more.
ans.look: Names both totals ($200 and $62) and says which is greater.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Give the reason for your choice. Use both totals.

a: 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 = 62, so Plan B pays $62 in total.
c) and d) Decision: Plan A, because $200 is more than $62.
items.hint: For Plan B, write the pay for each day in a row. Then add the five amounts.

items.q: The same neighbor now needs help for 10 days and offers the same two plans. Plan A pays $40 every day. Plan B pays $2 on day 1, and the pay doubles every day after that: day 2 pays $4, day 3 pays $8, and so on.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Total pay for the 10 days under Plan A

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Pay on day 10 alone under Plan B

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Total pay for the 10 days under Plan B

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Which plan should you take for this 10 day job?

ans.model: Plan A pays $400 in total. Plan B pays $2,046 in total, so Plan B pays $1,646 more. Day 10 alone pays $1,024, which is already more than all of Plan A.
ans.look: Names both totals ($400 and $2,046), or compares $400 with the $1,024 paid on day 10 alone.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Give the reason for your choice. Use the numbers.

a: d) and e) Decision: Plan B, because $2,046 is more than $400. Doubling starts small and then passes the fixed amount.
items.hint: List the pay for each day by doubling, and write the day number above each amount.

items.q: A family wants to pave a patio. Paving costs $8 for each square foot, and the budget is $1,100. Design 1 is a square that is 12 feet on each side. Design 2 is a rectangle that is 9 feet by 15 feet.

ans.model: Design 1 costs $1,152, which is $52 over the $1,100 budget. Design 2 costs $1,080, which is $20 under the budget, so only Design 2 fits.
ans.look: Names both costs and compares each one with $1,100.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Give the reason for your choice. Use both costs.

a: a) 12² = 144, so the square is 144 square feet.
c) 9 × 15 = 135, so the rectangle is 135 square feet.
1,152 − 1,100 = 52, so Design 1 is $52 over the budget.
1,100 − 1,080 = 20, so Design 2 is $20 under the budget.
d) and e) Decision: Design 2, because $1,080 is within the $1,100 budget and $1,152 is not.
items.hint: Find the area of each design in square feet before you find any cost.

items.q: A class trip costs $12 for each of 3 adults and $7 for each of 24 students. The group gets $20 off the total. Maya writes the cost as 3 × 12 + 24 × 7 − 20. Omar writes it as (3 × 12 + 24) × 7 − 20.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Whose expression matches the real cost of the trip?

options: No, the class needs more money

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The class has collected $190. Is that enough to pay for the trip?

ans.model: The adults cost 3 × 12 = $36 and the students cost 24 × 7 = $168. After the $20 discount the trip costs $184, which is the value of Maya's expression. Omar's parentheses multiply the adult cost by 7 as well, so his total is too high. $190 is $6 more than $184, so the class has enough.
ans.look: Says the trip costs $184, explains what Omar's parentheses change, and compares $184 with $190.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Give the reason for your two choices. Use the numbers.

a: c) Maya's expression matches, because each adult pays $12 once and each student pays $7 once.
d) 190 − 184 = 6, so $190 is enough and $6 is left over.
e) Decision: use Maya's expression. The trip costs $184, and the $190 covers it.
items.hint: In Maya's expression, do both multiplications before you add or subtract. In Omar's, finish the parentheses first.

sections.name: Part I: Stretch
sections.desc: Competition-style problems. Look for a pattern before you compute.

items.q: The ones digits of the powers of 3 follow a pattern. Here are the first five powers: 3¹ is 3, 3² is 9, 3³ is 27, 3⁴ is 81 and 3⁵ is 243.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: What is the ones digit of 3⁶?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The ones digits repeat in a cycle. How many digits are in the cycle before it starts over?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: What is the ones digit of 3²⁰?

a: a) 243 × 3 = 729, so the ones digit of 3⁶ is 9.
b) The ones digits go 3, 9, 7, 1, and then 3, 9, 7, 1 again. The cycle has 4 digits.
c) 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so 3²⁰ comes at the end of the fifth full cycle. Every full cycle ends in the digit 1.
items.hint: Write only the ones digit of each power in a row. Keep going until the digits start over.

items.q: 2 raised to which exponent has the same value as 4³?
items.hint: Find the value of the power of 4 first. Then build that value by multiplying 2s, and count them.

items.q: Look at the expression 2 + 3 × 4² − 6.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the value of 2 + 3 × 4² − 6 as it is written.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Which placement of parentheses changes the value to 74?

items.hint: Test each choice with the order of operations and write its value next to it.

items.q: Add the odd numbers in order, starting from 1, and look at the sums: 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 and 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write your answer to part a as a power with exponent 2. Type it with the ^ key.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Use the pattern to find the sum of the first 10 odd numbers, 1 + 3 + 5 and so on up to 19.

a: b) 36 = 6 × 6 = 6², so adding the first 6 odd numbers gives 6².
c) 10² = 100, so adding the first 10 odd numbers gives 100.
items.hint: Compare each sum with how many odd numbers were added to make it.

items.q: One cell splits into 2 cells every hour. After 1 hour there are 2 cells, after 2 hours there are 4 cells, and after 3 hours there are 8 cells.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: How many cells are there after 6 hours?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: After how many hours are there more than 1,000 cells for the first time?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: After 20 hours there are 2²⁰ cells. Twenty 2s multiplied together is the same as ten 2s times ten 2s, which is 2¹⁰ × 2¹⁰. Find the value of 2²⁰.

a: a) 2⁶ = 64, so there are 64 cells after 6 hours.
2¹⁰ = 1,024, which is more than 1,000, so the first time is after 10 hours.
items.hint: Keep doubling and number each step with its hour. Stop the first time you pass 1,000.

note: A power is a short way to write repeated multiplication: 3⁴ means 3 × 3 × 3 × 3. When an expression mixes operations, everyone follows one order: parentheses, exponents, multiply and divide from left to right, then add and subtract from left to right.

scene.title: Where you will see this
text: Powers show up wherever something keeps doubling or keeps growing by the same factor. If you send a photo to 2 friends, and each person who gets it sends it to 2 more, the third round of sending reaches 2 × 2 × 2 new people, and each round doubles again. Phone and tablet storage usually comes in sizes that are powers of 2 (32, 64, 128, 256 gigabytes). Money and measurement use powers of 10: there are 10² cents in a dollar, 10³ meters in a kilometer, and 10⁶ is one million.

Squares and cubes come from space. A square floor 12 feet on each side has 12² square feet of area, and a cube shaped box 3 feet on each side holds 3³ cubic feet. The order of operations is the agreement that lets a spreadsheet, a scientific calculator and a scientist all read 3 + 4 × 5 the same way. Without that agreement, two people could get two different totals from the same line. A simple calculator that works each key as you press it may skip the agreement, so the order is worth knowing yourself.
scene.ask: Before you start: find the storage size of a phone, tablet or computer at home, in gigabytes (look in Settings or on the box). Check whether the number is in this list of powers of 2: 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512.

scene_key: Not graded. Most devices show 32, 64, 128, 256 or 512 GB, which are 2⁵, 2⁶, 2⁷, 2⁸ and 2⁹. If his device shows a different number, ask him which power of 2 is closest. The point is that he sees powers of 2 on a real object before the first question.

text: In 3⁴, the 3 is the base and the 4 is the exponent. The exponent tells how many times the base is used as a factor: 3⁴ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3.
The exponent does not mean multiply by it. 3⁴ is 81, and 3 × 4 is only 12.

Exponent 2 is called squared (5² is 5 squared) and exponent 3 is called cubed (2³ is 2 cubed). Exponent 1 uses the base one time: 7¹ = 7. For powers of 10, the exponent tells how many zeros follow the 1: 10³ = 1,000.

steps: Multiply one step at a time: 6 × 6 = 36, then 36 × 6 = 216.

text: When an expression has more than one operation, work in this order.
1. Parentheses: do what is inside them first.
2. Exponents: find the value of each power.
3. Multiply and divide, from left to right.
4. Add and subtract, from left to right.
Rewrite the whole expression after every step. One step per line makes a slip easy to find.

steps: Parentheses first: 7 − 4 = 3. The expression is now 5 + 2 × 3².
Exponent next: 3² = 9. The expression is now 5 + 2 × 9.

text: Trap 1. Multiplying and dividing are partners, and so are adding and subtracting. Take each pair from left to right, in the order they appear. In 30 ÷ 5 × 2 the division comes first because it is on the left: 30 ÷ 5 = 6, then 6 × 2 = 12.
Trap 2. An exponent belongs only to the number it sits on. In 3 × 8² only the 8 is squared: 3 × 64 = 192. To square the whole product you need parentheses: (3 × 8)² = 24² = 576.

steps: Subtraction is first from the left: 20 − 8 = 12.
Adding first would take away 13 and leave 7. That breaks the left to right rule.
